items.quote: Should I give up my fruit, so good and sweet, to hold sway over the trees?
items.contrast: Giving up its good, sweet fruit versus the later consequence that the trees ask the vine.
items.reason: The fig tree presents surrendering its fruit as the cost of ruling. The trees turning to the vine happens afterward and is not its reason for refusing.

items.quote: Azariah the priest with eighty other courageous priests of the Lord followed him in. They confronted King Uzziah
items.contrast: King Uzziah as the person followed versus Azariah as one of those doing the following.
items.reason: The priests follow “him” after Uzziah enters the temple, and their confrontation identifies that person as King Uzziah.

items.quote: Uzziah rested with his ancestors and was buried near them in a cemetery that belonged to the kings, for people said, “He had leprosy.” And Jotham his son succeeded him as king.
items.contrast: Jotham succeeding Uzziah after the burial versus Isaiah recording Uzziah’s reign before the burial is narrated.
items.reason: The sequence places Jotham’s succession immediately after Uzziah’s burial. Isaiah’s recording is mentioned earlier.

items.quote: We have seen the land, and it is very good. Aren’t you going to do something? Don’t hesitate to go there and take it over.
items.contrast: The land as what is taken over versus the unsuspecting people who inhabit it.
items.reason: “It” refers back to the land they have seen. The people are described as those they will find there, not as the object of “take it over.”

items.quote: Paul spoke to the people and, because he intended to leave the next day, kept on talking until midnight.
items.contrast: Paul’s planned departure the next day as the reason for speaking so long versus the lamps as an incidental feature of the room.
items.reason: The clause beginning “because” directly gives Paul’s intended departure as the cause of his prolonged speaking. The lamps are not causally connected to it.
